Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Cologne/Perfume): A specific perfume or cologne, Somatic (Pain): Physical pain in a part of the body, Sexual Situations: Sexual situations or intimacy
  Maladaptive Strategies: Dissociation: I pretend it happened to someone else, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event, Body Monitoring: constantly check body for signs of danger or injury
  Threat: Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body

Vignette:
Three years ago, Tariq was waiting to change after his evening shift at the downtown gym when a man he did not know followed him into the vacant second-floor locker room. The air grew thick with a sharp, expensive cologne before fingers dug into Tariq’s hips and forced him against the cold tile. The man’s grip bruised the right side of his torso, and the assault was brief, brutal, and suffocating. Tariq remembers the exact scent, the way his own body had locked up in protest, and the lingering ache in his right ribs that refused to fade. That specific cologne and that particular spot of pain became inextricably tied to the violation, grounding his terror in a physical reality that refused to dissolve. When he returned home, the cologne from the stranger clung to the memory like a stain. Days turned into weeks, and Tariq found himself stopping dead in grocery store aisles or on city sidewalks whenever that same woody, citrus cologne drifted past. His right ribs would throb with a familiar, phantom soreness, a somatic echo that made him press his palms flat against the wall until the sensation passed. What frightened him most was the shame that settled over his skin; he began to view his own body as compromised, a place that had failed him and now bore the mark of what happened to it. He convinced himself he would never feel normal emotions again, that something inside him had been permanently severed. To keep the memories at bay, Tariq stopped thinking about that night entirely. When images tried to surface, he told himself they belonged to a man he once knew, not him. He began constantly checking his torso and shoulders for new injuries or unusual tightness, running his hands over his muscles until he confirmed they were unmarked. The avoidance extended to his marriage. He and his wife, Layla, had always been physically close, but the moment intimacy shifted toward anything resembling the assault, Tariq would pull away. He started making excuses—fatigue, workload, sore muscles—until they grew accustomed to sleeping back-to-back. Over the months, these habits hardened. The clinic where he worked as a physical therapist became a landscape of constant vigilance. During treatment sessions, Tariq found himself monitoring his own posture and breathing as much as his patients’, his hands trembling slightly when a patient shifted suddenly in a chair or when a colleague patted his shoulder without warning. He reacted to the unexpected movements and touches with a jolt, his heart hammering against his right ribs, certain that danger was imminent. He could not rely on himself to stay steady, especially when a new client walked in wearing that familiar cologne. He told himself his own body was no longer trustworthy, and that the shame of what had happened to it meant he could not be relied upon to protect his own life or his marriage. The cologne avoidance, the body checks, and the emotional distance simply ran parallel, each occupying his attention. He began turning down double shifts, citing safety concerns when he really meant he could not bear the confined staff rooms. Layla noticed his withdrawal and asked him to speak with someone, but Tariq only felt more certain that he was broken beyond repair. When a junior therapist startled him during a walkthrough, causing him to drop a stack of therapy bands and flinch violently, the illusion of control finally shattered. He booked an appointment that week. Sitting across from the clinician, Tariq clutched his hands together, bracing for the shame he expected, hoping quietly that someone might help him untangle the fear from his own skin before it pulled him entirely under.
